## Transactional Email

Send one-off transactional messages.


send_transactional_email(subscriber_email: str | list[str], template_id: int, from_email: str | None = None, template_data: dict[str, Any] | None = None, messenger_channel: str = 'email', content_type: str = 'markdown', altbody: str | None = None, attachments: list[pathlib.Path] | None = None, email_headers: list[dict[str, str | None]] | None = None, timeout_config: httpx2.Timeout | None = None, subscriber_mode: Literal['default', 'fallback', 'external'] | None = None) -> bool

Send a transactional email through Listmonk to one or more recipients.

By default the recipient must already be a subscriber on at least one list
(see subscriber_mode to relax this). Delivery errors may surface in the logs
section of your Listmonk dashboard rather than as exceptions here. Recipient
addresses are lowercased and stripped before sending.

Args:
    subscriber_email: The recipient's email address, or a list of addresses to
        send to several recipients in one call. By default each recipient must
        already be a subscriber of some list on your server; see subscriber_mode
        to relax that. Addresses are lowercased and stripped.
    template_id: The ID of the template to render. Required. Must be a 'tx'
        (transactional) template, not a campaign template.
    from_email: The From address. Omit to use the default address at your
        sending provider.
    template_data: Merge parameters available in the template as {{ .Tx.Data.* }}.
        Defaults to an empty dict.
    messenger_channel: The delivery channel. Defaults to 'email'; use another
        configured channel (e.g. SMS) if available.
    content_type: The body format: 'html', 'markdown', or 'plain'.
        Defaults to 'markdown'.
    altbody: Optional alternate plain-text body for multipart HTML emails.
    attachments: Optional list of pathlib.Path objects pointing to files to
        attach. Each path must exist and be a file.
    email_headers: Optional list of custom headers, each a single-entry dict,
        e.g. [{'X-Custom': 'value'}].
    timeout_config: Optional per-request timeout; defaults to 10 seconds.
    subscriber_mode: How the server resolves each recipient, on Listmonk
        servers that support it. One of 'default', 'fallback', or 'external'.
        Omit it (None) and the field is left off the request entirely, so the
        server keeps its own default behavior of requiring a subscriber.
        'fallback' looks the recipient up but sends anyway if not found.
        'external' skips the lookup, so you can send to non-subscribers. In
        'fallback' and 'external' modes, subscriber fields other than the email
        are unavailable in templates; use {{ .Tx.Data.* }} instead.

Returns:
    True if the server accepted the send, False otherwise.

Raises:
    ValueError: If no recipient is given, or if a recipient list is empty or
        contains only blank addresses.
    ListmonkFileNotFoundError: If any attachment path does not exist or is not a file.
    OperationNotAllowedError: If the base URL has not been set or you have not logged in.
    httpx2.HTTPStatusError: If the server responds with a 4xx or 5xx status.
    ValidationError: If the response is empty or is not valid JSON.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    ...     subscriber_email='person@example.com',
    ...     template_id=3,
    ...     template_data={'name': 'Sam'},
    ... )
    True

    Send to several people who need not be subscribers:

    >>> listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    ...     ['one@example.com', 'two@example.com'],
    ...     template_id=3,
    ...     subscriber_mode='external',
    ... )
    True


## Data Models

Pydantic models returned by and passed to the API functions.


MailingList(*, id: int, created_at: datetime.datetime, updated_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, uuid: str, name: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, optin: str | None = None, tags: list[str], description: str | None = None, subscriber_count: int | None = None, subscriber_statuses: listmonk.models.SubscriberStatus | None = None) -> None

A mailing list on the Listmonk instance.

Attributes:
    id: The numeric list ID assigned by Listmonk.
    created_at: When the list was created.
    updated_at: When the list was last modified, if ever.
    uuid: The globally unique identifier for the list.
    name: The human-readable list name.
    type: The list visibility, typically ``public`` or ``private``.
    optin: The opt-in mode, either ``single`` or ``double``.
    tags: Arbitrary labels attached to the list.
    description: A free-text description of the list.
    subscriber_count: The total number of subscribers on the list.
    subscriber_statuses: A breakdown of subscriber counts by subscription status.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> lst = listmonk.list_by_id(7)
    >>> lst.name, lst.optin, lst.subscriber_count
    ('Course Announcements', 'double', 1250)

SubscriberStatus(*, unconfirmed: int | None = None) -> None

A breakdown of subscriber counts by subscription status for a mailing list.

Attributes:
    unconfirmed_count: The number of subscriptions still awaiting double opt-in
        confirmation (read from the API's ``unconfirmed`` field).

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> lst = listmonk.list_by_id(7)
    >>> lst.subscriber_statuses.unconfirmed_count
    5

SubscriberStatuses(*values)

The global status of a subscriber on the Listmonk instance.

Attributes:
    enabled: The subscriber is active and will receive campaigns.
    disabled: The subscriber is paused and will not receive campaigns.
    blocklisted: The subscriber has been blocked and will not receive any mail.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from listmonk.models import SubscriberStatuses
    >>> sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('some_user@talkpython.fm')
    >>> listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, status=SubscriberStatuses.disabled).status
    'disabled'

Subscriber(*, id: int, email: str, name: str | None = None, created_at: datetime.datetime, updated_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, uuid: str | None = None, lists: list[dict[str, typing.Any]] = <factory>, attribs: dict[str, typing.Any] = <factory>, status: str | None = None) -> None

A subscriber (contact) on the Listmonk instance.

Attributes:
    id: The numeric subscriber ID assigned by Listmonk.
    email: The subscriber's email address (their primary identifier).
    name: The subscriber's display name, if provided.
    created_at: When the subscriber was created.
    updated_at: When the subscriber was last modified, if ever.
    uuid: The globally unique identifier for the subscriber.
    lists: The lists this subscriber belongs to, each as a dict describing the
        membership (list id, subscription status, and so on). Serialization via
        ``model_dump()`` emits plain list IDs.
    attribs: Arbitrary custom attributes stored against the subscriber.
    status: The subscriber's global status, e.g. ``enabled``, ``disabled``, or ``blocklisted``.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('some_user@talkpython.fm')
    >>> sub.attribs['city'], [lst['id'] for lst in sub.lists]
    ('Portland', [1, 4])

CreateSubscriberModel(*, email: str, name: str | None = None, status: str, lists: list[int] = <factory>, preconfirm_subscriptions: bool, attribs: dict[str, typing.Any] = <factory>) -> None

The payload used to create a new subscriber.

This is the raw request body sent to Listmonk. The higher-level
``create_subscriber`` helper populates it (always sending ``status='enabled'``),
and ``update_subscriber`` reuses it as the full PUT body when updating an
existing subscriber (with the caller-supplied status).

Attributes:
    email: The email address for the new subscriber (required).
    name: The subscriber's display name, if any.
    status: The initial global status (required), e.g. ``enabled``, ``disabled``,
        or ``blocklisted``.
    lists: The IDs of the lists to subscribe this person to. Defaults to an empty list.
    preconfirm_subscriptions: Required flag; when ``True``, mark the new subscriptions as
        confirmed immediately (skipping double opt-in confirmation emails).
    attribs: Arbitrary custom attributes to store against the subscriber. Defaults to an empty dict.

Examples:
    >>> from listmonk.models import CreateSubscriberModel
    >>> payload = CreateSubscriberModel(
    ...     email='some_user@talkpython.fm', status='enabled', preconfirm_subscriptions=True
    ... )
    >>> payload.model_dump()['lists']
    []

Campaign(*, id: int, created_at: datetime.datetime, updated_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, views: int, clicks: int, lists: list[dict[str, typing.Any]] = <factory>, started_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, to_send: int, sent: int, uuid: str, name: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, subject: str | None = None, from_email: str | None = None, body: str | None = None, altbody: str | None = None, send_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, status: str | None = None, content_type: str | None = None, tags: list[str] = <factory>, template_id: int, messenger: str | None = None, headers: list[dict[str, str | None]] = <factory>, media: list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None) -> None

An email campaign on the Listmonk instance.

Attributes:
    id: The numeric campaign ID assigned by Listmonk.
    created_at: When the campaign was created.
    updated_at: When the campaign was last modified, if ever.
    views: The number of times the campaign has been opened/viewed.
    clicks: The number of link clicks recorded for the campaign.
    lists: The target lists for the campaign, each as a dict describing the list.
    started_at: When sending began, if the campaign has started.
    to_send: The total number of recipients the campaign will be sent to.
    sent: The number of messages sent so far.
    uuid: The globally unique identifier for the campaign.
    name: The internal campaign name.
    type: The campaign type, e.g. ``regular`` or ``optin``.
    subject: The email subject line.
    from_email: The sender (From) address.
    body: The campaign body in the configured content type.
    altbody: The optional plain-text alternative body for multipart HTML emails.
    send_at: The scheduled send time, if the campaign is scheduled.
    status: The campaign status, e.g. ``draft``, ``scheduled``, ``running``,
        ``paused``, ``cancelled``, or ``finished``.
    content_type: The body format, e.g. ``richtext``, ``html``, ``markdown``, or ``plain``.
    tags: Arbitrary labels attached to the campaign.
    template_id: The ID of the template used to render the campaign.
    messenger: The delivery channel, typically ``email``.
    headers: Custom email headers to include, each as a single-entry dict.
    media: The media files attached to the campaign, each as a dict describing
        the file (id, filename, and so on), or ``None`` if there are none.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> campaign = listmonk.campaign_by_id(7)
    >>> campaign.status, campaign.sent, campaign.to_send
    ('draft', 0, 1500)

CampaignStatuses(*values)

The lifecycle status of a campaign.

Attributes:
    draft: Created but not queued; safe to edit.
    scheduled: Will start automatically at the campaign's send_at time.
    running: Actively sending to the target lists.
    paused: Sending has been halted and can be resumed.
    cancelled: Sending was stopped and will not resume.
    finished: All messages have been sent.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from listmonk.models import CampaignStatuses
    >>> listmonk.set_campaign_status(7, CampaignStatuses.running).status
    'running'

CreateCampaignModel(*, name: str | None = None, subject: str | None = None, lists: list[int] = <factory>, from_email: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, content_type: str | None = None, body: str | None = None, altbody: str | None = None, send_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, messenger: str | None = None, template_id: int | None, tags: list[str] = <factory>, headers: list[dict[str, str | None]] = <factory>, media: list[int] = <factory>) -> None

The payload used to create a new campaign.

This is the raw request body sent to Listmonk; the higher-level
``create_campaign`` helper validates that name and subject are present and
defaults the target list to ``{1}`` before populating this model.

Attributes:
    name: The internal campaign name.
    subject: The email subject line.
    lists: The IDs of the lists to send the campaign to. Defaults to an empty list.
    from_email: The sender (From) address. Omit to use the instance default.
    type: The campaign type, e.g. ``regular`` or ``optin``.
    content_type: The body format, e.g. ``richtext``, ``html``, ``markdown``, or ``plain``.
    body: The campaign body in the configured content type.
    altbody: The optional plain-text alternative body for multipart HTML emails.
    send_at: The scheduled send time, if the campaign should be scheduled. Serialized to
        an ISO-8601 string (or ``None``) when sent.
    messenger: The delivery channel, typically ``email``.
    template_id: The ID of the template used to render the campaign. Required field that
        may be ``None`` (it has no default and must be supplied explicitly).
    tags: Arbitrary labels to attach to the campaign. Defaults to an empty list.
    headers: Custom email headers to include, each as a single-entry dict. Defaults to an empty list.
    media: The IDs of uploaded media files to attach to the campaign. Defaults to an empty list.

Examples:
    >>> from listmonk.models import CreateCampaignModel
    >>> payload = CreateCampaignModel(name='June', subject='Our June Update', lists=[1], template_id=None)
    >>> payload.model_dump()['template_id'] is None
    True

UpdateCampaignModel(*, name: str | None = None, subject: str | None = None, lists: list[int] = <factory>, from_email: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, content_type: str | None = None, body: str | None = None, altbody: str | None = None, send_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, messenger: str | None = None, template_id: int | None, tags: list[str] = <factory>, headers: list[dict[str, str | None]] = <factory>, media: list[int] = <factory>) -> None

The payload used to update an existing campaign.

Shares all fields with ``CreateCampaignModel``. As a safeguard, a ``send_at``
value that is already in the past is dropped (set to ``None``) before sending,
so that updating a campaign does not fail on a stale scheduled time.

Examples:
    >>> import datetime
    >>> from listmonk.models import UpdateCampaignModel
    >>> stale = datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
    >>> UpdateCampaignModel(template_id=1, send_at=stale).send_at is None
    True

CampaignPreview(*, preview: str | None = None) -> None

A rendered preview of a campaign.

Attributes:
    preview: The rendered HTML preview of the campaign body.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> preview = listmonk.campaign_preview_by_id(7)
    >>> preview.preview[:15]
    '<!doctype html>'

Template(*, id: int, created_at: datetime.datetime, updated_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, name: str | None = None, subject: str | None = None, body: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, is_default: bool | None = None) -> None

An email template on the Listmonk instance.

Attributes:
    id: The numeric template ID assigned by Listmonk.
    created_at: When the template was created.
    updated_at: When the template was last modified, if ever.
    name: The template name.
    subject: The default subject line for the template, if any.
    body: The template body markup.
    type: The template type, e.g. ``campaign`` or ``tx`` (transactional).
    is_default: Whether this is the default template for its type.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> tmpl = listmonk.template_by_id(3)
    >>> tmpl.type, tmpl.is_default
    ('tx', False)

CreateTemplateModel(*, name: str | None = None, subject: str | None = None, body: str | None = None, type: str | None = None, is_default: bool | None = False) -> None

The payload used to create a new template.

Attributes:
    name: The template name.
    subject: The default subject line for the template, if any.
    body: The template body markup.
    type: The template type, e.g. ``campaign`` or ``tx`` (transactional).
    is_default: Whether the new template should become the default for its type. Defaults to ``False``.

Examples:
    >>> from listmonk.models import CreateTemplateModel
    >>> payload = CreateTemplateModel(name='Welcome', body='Hi {{ template "content" . }}', type='tx')
    >>> payload.model_dump()['is_default']
    False

TemplatePreview(*, preview: str | None = None) -> None

A rendered preview of a template.

Attributes:
    preview: The rendered HTML preview of the template, using lorem-ipsum sample content.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> preview = listmonk.template_preview_by_id(3)
    >>> preview.preview[:15]
    '<!doctype html>'

Media(*, id: int, uuid: str, filename: str | None = None, content_type: str | None = None, created_at: datetime.datetime | None = None, uri: str | None = None, thumb_uri: str | None = None) -> None

A file uploaded to the Listmonk media library.

Attributes:
    id: The numeric media ID assigned by Listmonk. Pass it to ``create_campaign``
        or ``update_campaign`` via ``media_ids`` to attach the file to a campaign.
    uuid: The globally unique identifier for the media file.
    filename: The name the file was stored under.
    content_type: The MIME type of the file, if reported by the server.
    created_at: When the file was uploaded.
    uri: The server path the uploaded file is served from.
    thumb_uri: The server path of the generated thumbnail, if any.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from pathlib import Path
    >>> media = listmonk.upload_media(Path('/path/to/chart.png'))
    >>> media.id, media.filename
    (11, 'chart.png')


## Exceptions

Errors raised by the client.


ValidationError

Raised when an argument fails client-side validation before a request is sent,
or when the server returns an empty or malformed JSON response.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from listmonk.errors import ValidationError
    >>> try:
    ...     listmonk.set_url_base('listmonk.somedomain.tech')  # no scheme
    ... except ValidationError as e:
    ...     print(e)
    The url must start with the HTTP scheme (http:// or https://).

OperationNotAllowedError

Raised when an operation is not permitted in the client's current state.

For example, calling an API before the base URL has been set, or before a successful login.
It subclasses ValidationError, so an ``except ValidationError`` clause catches it too.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from listmonk.errors import OperationNotAllowedError
    >>> try:
    ...     listmonk.lists()  # before set_url_base() and login()
    ... except OperationNotAllowedError as e:
    ...     print(e)
    URL Base must be set to proceed.

ListmonkFileNotFoundError

Raised when a local file referenced for upload (e.g. a transactional email attachment) cannot be found.

Examples:
    >>> import listmonk
    >>> from pathlib import Path
    >>> from listmonk.errors import ListmonkFileNotFoundError
    >>> try:
    ...     listmonk.upload_media(Path('/no/such/chart.png'))
    ... except ListmonkFileNotFoundError as e:
    ...     print(e)
    File /no/such/chart.png does not exist


----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Get started

## What you are connecting to

[Listmonk](https://listmonk.app) is a self-hosted mail platform: subscribers, mailing lists, campaigns, templates, and a transactional endpoint for the one-off emails your app sends when something happens. It has a thorough [REST API](https://listmonk.app/docs/apis/apis/). This package wraps the part of that API most applications reach for every day, so your Python code can say "subscribe this person", "send them this", and "start that campaign" without hand-building requests.

It is a flat module, not a client class. You configure it once, then call functions on `listmonk` directly. That keeps the common case down to three lines.

## Install

```bash
pip install listmonk
```

Or `uv add listmonk`. It needs Python 3.10 or newer and pulls in [httpx2](https://github.com/pydantic/httpx2) for HTTP, [Pydantic](https://pydantic.dev) for the models, and `strenum` for the status enums. The package ships `py.typed`, so mypy and pyright see the real signatures.

## Create an API user

Recent Listmonk versions want API access to go through a dedicated API user rather than your own login. In the Listmonk admin, open Users, create a user of type API, and copy the token it shows you; that token is the password you will pass to `login()`.

The role you attach to that user decides what the client is allowed to do. For everything in this guide the role needs read and manage rights on subscribers, lists, campaigns, templates, and media, plus `subscribers:sql_query`. That last one is easy to forget and is behind the most common error people hit; see [Errors and troubleshooting](error-handling.qmd#forbidden-403) for how it shows up.

## First contact

```python
import listmonk

listmonk.set_url_base('https://listmonk.your.domain')

if not listmonk.login('api_user', 'the-token-from-listmonk'):
    raise SystemExit('Listmonk rejected the credentials or is unreachable.')

print(listmonk.is_healthy())  # True
```

Three things are happening here.

[`set_url_base()`](../reference/set_url_base.qmd) stores the address of your instance. It wants the scheme (`https://`) and nothing after the host, so no `/api` and no trailing path. It strips a trailing slash for you and raises `ValidationError` if the scheme is missing.

[`login()`](../reference/login.qmd) checks the credentials by calling Listmonk's health endpoint with HTTP Basic auth, then stores them at module level. Every later call reuses them, so this is a once-at-startup call. Notice that it returns a bool. A `False` means either the server said no or the server could not be reached at all; it does not raise for either. Check the bool.

[`is_healthy()`](../reference/is_healthy.qmd) is the same health call, available any time you want to confirm the instance is up and the stored credentials still work. [`verify_login()`](../reference/verify_login.qmd) is an alias for it.

Until `set_url_base()` and a successful `login()` have both happened, every other function raises `listmonk.errors.OperationNotAllowedError`. If you see that error, the configuration calls were skipped, ran in a different process, or `login()` returned `False` and nobody checked.

## Your first real call

```python
sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('someone@example.com')

if sub is None:
    sub = listmonk.create_subscriber('someone@example.com', 'Someone', list_ids={1}, pre_confirm=True)

print(sub.id, sub.status, [lst['id'] for lst in sub.lists])
```

That is the shape of most work with this library: look something up, get a Pydantic model back (or `None` when there is no match), create or change it, and get the server's fresh copy back. The rest of the guide walks through each area.

## Where to go next

- [Subscribers](subscribers.qmd): create, find, update, pause, unsubscribe, and delete people, and query them by custom attributes.
- [Lists and segmentation](lists.qmd): create and reshape lists, bulk membership, and opt-in confirmation.
- [Transactional email](transactional-email.qmd): password resets, receipts, and invites, including to people who are not subscribers.
- [Campaigns](campaigns.qmd): the campaign life cycle from draft to sent, with media, previews, and test sends.
- [Templates](templates.qmd): the frame around every message, and the one rule every template must follow.
- [Recipes](recipes.qmd): copy-ready handlers for signup forms, unsubscribe links, receipts, and syncing your user table.
- [Errors and troubleshooting](error-handling.qmd): which calls raise, which return `False` or `None`, and what the common errors mean.
- [Testing your integration](testing.qmd): fake the server so your app's tests never touch a real Listmonk.
- [How it works](how-it-works.qmd): module-level state, httpx2, the models, and what the client does not cover.


### Errors and troubleshooting

Bad news arrives in two shapes in this library. Some calls raise. Others hand you a `False` or a `None` and expect you to look. Knowing which shape a call uses is the difference between a `try/except` that works and one that never fires.

## Calls that raise

Every data call checks the client state first and raises `listmonk.errors.OperationNotAllowedError` if [`set_url_base()`](../reference/set_url_base.qmd) or a successful [`login()`](../reference/login.qmd) has not happened yet.

Bad arguments raise `ValueError` before any request is sent: an empty email in `create_subscriber()`, a template body without the `{{ template "content" . }}` placeholder, a list type that is not `public` or `private`, a campaign with no name or subject.

A 4xx or 5xx response from the server raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. The exception carries the response, so `e.response.status_code` and `e.response.text` tell you what Listmonk said. Note the module name: this library uses [httpx2](https://github.com/pydantic/httpx2), the Pydantic-maintained fork of httpx, so catch `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. An `httpx.HTTPStatusError` handler will not match.

An empty response body, or one that is not JSON (a proxy's HTML error page, say), raises `listmonk.errors.ValidationError`. `OperationNotAllowedError` is a subclass of it, so one `except ValidationError` clause catches both.

A missing attachment path in `send_transactional_email()` or `upload_media()` raises `listmonk.errors.ListmonkFileNotFoundError`, a subclass of the built-in `FileNotFoundError`.

## Calls that return a value instead

| Call | Returns | When |
| ---- | ------- | ---- |
| `login()`, `is_healthy()`, `verify_login()` | `False` | Credentials rejected, or the server unreachable. Never raises for these. |
| `confirm_optin()`, `add_subscribers_to_lists()` | `False` | Any non-2xx response. `add_subscribers_to_lists()` also returns `False` for empty inputs. |
| `subscriber_by_email()`, `subscriber_by_id()`, `subscriber_by_uuid()`, `campaign_by_id()`, `template_by_id()` | `None` | Nothing matches. |
| `set_campaign_status()`, `start_campaign()`, `pause_campaign()`, `cancel_campaign()` | `None` | No campaign has that ID. |
| `delete_subscriber()`, `delete_campaign()`, `delete_template()`, `test_campaign()` | `False` | The target does not exist. |
| `update_subscriber()`, `update_campaign()`, `update_template()` | `None` | The follow-up fetch after a successful update finds nothing. Rare. |

The odd one out is [`list_by_id()`](../reference/list_by_id.qmd), which returns a `MailingList` rather than an optional and raises if the list is missing.

```python
import httpx2
import listmonk
from listmonk.errors import OperationNotAllowedError, ValidationError

try:
    subscriber = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('someone@some.domain')
except OperationNotAllowedError:
    ...  # call set_url_base() and login() first
except httpx2.HTTPStatusError as e:
    ...  # e.response.status_code, e.response.text
except ValidationError:
    ...  # the server answered with something that is not JSON

if subscriber is None:
    ...  # no such subscriber; not an error
```

## Timeouts

Every network call accepts `timeout_config`, an `httpx2.Timeout`, and defaults to 10 seconds. A slow or far-away instance, or a `subscribers()` call that pages through a large list, may need more:

```python
import httpx2

everyone = listmonk.subscribers(timeout_config=httpx2.Timeout(timeout=60))
```

A timeout surfaces as an `httpx2.TimeoutException` from the underlying request.

## OperationNotAllowedError: You must login before proceeding

Authentication is module-level state. Call `set_url_base(url)` and then `login(user, password)` once at startup, before any other function, and check that `login()` returned `True`. A `False` return means the server rejected the credentials or could not be reached; no exception is raised in that case, which is why skipping the check leads here.

If your app runs under several worker processes, each process has its own copy of that state and each needs to log in. A fixture or startup hook is the usual place.

## Forbidden (403)

```text
httpx2.HTTPStatusError: Client error '403 Forbidden' for url 'https://yoursite.local/api/subscribers?page=1&per_page=100&query=subscribers.email='john@example.com''
```

Your password was fine; a bad one makes `login()` return `False` much earlier. The `query=` in the URL is the clue: this is a SQL-filtered subscriber lookup, and the API user's role lacks the `subscribers:sql_query` permission. Listmonk requires it whenever a `query` parameter is sent. Add the permission to the role in Users and Roles and retry. The [Listmonk roles documentation](https://listmonk.app/docs/roles-and-permissions/#user-roles) has the details.

Which calls need it: [`subscribers(query_text=...)`](../reference/subscribers.qmd), [`subscriber_by_email()`](../reference/subscriber_by_email.qmd), and [`subscriber_by_uuid()`](../reference/subscriber_by_uuid.qmd). Which do not: [`subscriber_by_id()`](../reference/subscriber_by_id.qmd), which uses Listmonk's direct per-subscriber endpoint, and `subscribers(list_id=...)` without a query.

A 403 from any other call means the role is missing the read or manage permission for that resource, or that the subscriber belongs to a list the API user may not see.

## test_campaign() raised 400: No known subscribers to test

Listmonk only sends campaign tests to addresses that already exist as subscribers. It does not create them, and when none of the addresses you passed are known it rejects the request with HTTP 400, which the client raises as `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. Create the subscriber first (`create_subscriber(email, pre_confirm=True)`) or use an address that is already on a list. See [Campaigns](campaigns.qmd#test-before-you-send).

## Campaign status change rejected (400)

`start_campaign()`, `pause_campaign()`, and `cancel_campaign()` ask the server for a specific transition, and Listmonk only allows some: draft to scheduled or running, scheduled to draft, running to paused or cancelled, paused to running. Starting a finished campaign or pausing a draft comes back as a 400. Read the campaign's `status` first if you are unsure where it is.

## HTTP 409 on create_subscriber()

The email already exists on the instance. Look the subscriber up with `subscriber_by_email()` and update them instead; the [signup form recipe](recipes.qmd#handle-a-signup-form) shows the pattern.

## SSL certificate verification failed

httpx2 validates TLS certificates against the bundled `certifi` CA list by default. If you self-host Listmonk behind a custom or corporate Certificate Authority you may see:

```text
ssl.SSLCertVerificationError: certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate
```

Point the client at your CA bundle through the standard environment variables before the library makes its first request:

```bash
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/path/to/your-ca-bundle.pem   # or SSL_CERT_DIR=/path/to/ca-dir
```

## A transactional email returned True but never arrived

`send_transactional_email()` returns `True` when Listmonk accepted the message for delivery. What happens after that (SMTP rejection, bounce, a messenger that is down) is reported in the Logs section of the Listmonk admin, not back to the client. Check there first, then the recipient's spam folder.



## Working with Listmonk

### Subscribers

A subscriber is a person: an email address, an optional name, a global status, a bag of custom attributes, and the lists they are on. Almost everything your app does with Listmonk starts here.

## Creating one

```python
sub = listmonk.create_subscriber(
    'jane@example.com',
    'Jane Doe',
    list_ids={1, 7},
    pre_confirm=True,
    attribs={'plan': 'pro', 'signup_source': 'webinar'},
)
print(sub.id, sub.uuid)
```

[`create_subscriber()`](../reference/create_subscriber.qmd) lowercases and strips the email, strips the name, and always creates the person with a global status of `enabled`. The `list_ids` set is optional. `pre_confirm=True` tells Listmonk that your app already obtained consent, so it marks the subscriptions confirmed and sends no double opt-in email; leave it off for a double opt-in list and Listmonk will ask the person to confirm. `attribs` is any JSON-serialisable dict and is stored as-is.

If the email already exists, Listmonk answers 409 and the client raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. Look the person up first when that is a possibility; the [signup recipe](recipes.qmd#handle-a-signup-form) does exactly that.

## Finding one

```python
by_email = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('jane@example.com')
by_id = listmonk.subscriber_by_id(201)
by_uuid = listmonk.subscriber_by_uuid('c37786af-e6ab-4260-9b49-740a8cd6a7ed')
```

All three return a [`Subscriber`](../reference/models.Subscriber.qmd) or `None`. They never raise just because nobody matched.

Two of them have a permission requirement worth knowing about. [`subscriber_by_email()`](../reference/subscriber_by_email.qmd) and [`subscriber_by_uuid()`](../reference/subscriber_by_uuid.qmd) send a server-side SQL filter, so the API user's role needs `subscribers:sql_query` or the server answers 403. [`subscriber_by_id()`](../reference/subscriber_by_id.qmd) uses Listmonk's direct per-subscriber endpoint and needs only ordinary read permission. The value you pass to the email and UUID lookups is sent as a quoted SQL literal with embedded quotes escaped, so user-supplied input cannot widen the match.

## Finding many

```python
on_the_list = listmonk.subscribers(list_id=7)
in_portland = listmonk.subscribers(query_text="subscribers.attribs->>'city' = 'Portland'")
both = listmonk.subscribers(query_text="subscribers.status = 'enabled'", list_id=7)
```

[`subscribers()`](../reference/subscribers.qmd) fetches every match, 500 per page, and joins the pages, ordered by `updated_at` descending. With no arguments it returns the whole instance, so give it a long `timeout_config` on a big one. The `query_text` is Listmonk's SQL-like filter over the `subscribers` table; custom attributes live in a JSONB column and are reached with `->>`. The [Listmonk querying docs](https://listmonk.app/docs/querying-and-segmentation/) cover the syntax. Filtering by `list_id` alone needs no special permission; passing `query_text` needs `subscribers:sql_query`.

Values you interpolate into `query_text` yourself are your responsibility. Quote them as SQL literals and never splice raw user input into the filter.

## Changing one

Updates follow one pattern across the whole library: fetch the model, change what you like, pass it back. The client sends the whole record to the server and returns the server's fresh copy.

```python
sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('jane@example.com')
sub.name = 'Jane A. Doe'
sub.attribs['plan'] = 'enterprise'
sub = listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, add_to_lists={4}, remove_from_lists={7})
```

[`update_subscriber()`](../reference/update_subscriber.qmd) works out list membership as "the lists she is on now, minus `remove_from_lists`, plus `add_to_lists`", and marks those subscriptions confirmed. Her global status is kept as it is unless you pass `status=`, so changing a blocklisted person's name does not put them back on your lists. The return value is the subscriber re-fetched from the server, or `None` in the unlikely case that the re-fetch finds nothing.

Because the whole record is sent, two callers updating the same subscriber at the same time will overwrite each other. Fetch, change, and update in one short sequence.

## Pausing, unsubscribing, and deleting

People pause, people leave, and sometimes people ask to be forgotten. Those are three different operations.

```python
sub = listmonk.disable_subscriber(sub)   # status 'disabled': delivery paused, reversible
sub = listmonk.enable_subscriber(sub)    # status 'enabled': back on

sub = listmonk.block_subscriber(sub)     # status 'blocklisted': the real unsubscribe

listmonk.delete_subscriber('jane@example.com')            # gone, by email
listmonk.delete_subscriber(overriding_subscriber_id=201)  # gone, by ID, no lookup first
```

[`disable_subscriber()`](../reference/disable_subscriber.qmd) and [`enable_subscriber()`](../reference/enable_subscriber.qmd) toggle delivery without touching anything else. [`block_subscriber()`](../reference/block_subscriber.qmd) is the proper unsubscribe: the record stays, so a later import cannot accidentally resurrect the person, but nothing is sent to them again. [`delete_subscriber()`](../reference/delete_subscriber.qmd) removes the record entirely and returns `False` if the email matched nobody.

If you only want to take someone off one list while leaving the others alone, that is not a status change at all; use `update_subscriber(sub, remove_from_lists={list_id})`. The [unsubscribe recipe](recipes.qmd#handle-an-unsubscribe-link) shows both paths side by side.

## Reading the model

A [`Subscriber`](../reference/models.Subscriber.qmd) carries `id`, `uuid`, `email`, `name`, `status`, `attribs`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, and `lists`. The `lists` field is a list of dicts straight from the server, each with the list `id`, `name`, and the `subscription_status` (`confirmed`, `unconfirmed`, or `unsubscribed`) for that membership. Calling `model_dump()` on a subscriber reduces `lists` to plain IDs and formats the timestamps the way the API expects, which is what `update_subscriber()` relies on.


### Lists and segmentation

Lists are how Listmonk decides who gets what. A campaign targets one or more lists; a subscriber belongs to any number of them. Most apps have a handful (the newsletter, the product announcements, the beta testers) and manage membership from code as people sign up, upgrade, and leave.

## Reading lists

```python
for lst in listmonk.lists():
    print(lst.id, lst.name, lst.type, lst.optin, lst.subscriber_count)

newsletter = listmonk.list_by_id(7)
```

[`lists()`](../reference/lists.qmd) returns every list on the instance in one request. [`list_by_id()`](../reference/list_by_id.qmd) returns a [`MailingList`](../reference/models.MailingList.qmd) and, unlike the subscriber lookups, raises rather than returning `None` when the ID is unknown. Each model carries the list's `uuid`, which you will need for opt-in confirmation below, and a `subscriber_statuses` breakdown with the count still awaiting confirmation.

## Creating and changing lists

```python
beta = listmonk.create_list('Beta testers', list_type='private', optin='single', tags=['product'])

listmonk.update_list(beta.id, description='People trying the new editor')
listmonk.update_list(beta.id, status='archived')

listmonk.delete_list(beta.id)
```

[`create_list()`](../reference/create_list.qmd) needs a name; `list_type` is `public` or `private` (public lists appear on Listmonk's public subscription form) and `optin` is `single` or `double`. Both are validated before the request goes out. [`update_list()`](../reference/update_list.qmd) sends only the fields you pass, so an update that mentions just `description` leaves everything else alone; `status` can move a list between `active` and `archived`. [`delete_list()`](../reference/delete_list.qmd) checks that the list exists first and raises if it does not.

## Membership

There are three ways to put people on lists, suited to three different moments.

At signup, pass `list_ids` to [`create_subscriber()`](../reference/create_subscriber.qmd).

For one person later on, use [`update_subscriber()`](../reference/update_subscriber.qmd) with `add_to_lists` and `remove_from_lists`. The result is the person's current lists, minus the removals, plus the additions.

For many people at once, use [`add_subscribers_to_lists()`](../reference/add_subscribers_to_lists.qmd):

```python
ok = listmonk.add_subscribers_to_lists([201, 202, 203], [7, 9])
ok = listmonk.add_subscribers_to_lists([201], [7], status='unconfirmed')
```

It de-duplicates both ID sets, marks the new subscriptions `confirmed` unless you say `unconfirmed`, and returns `False` rather than raising when either set is empty or the server answers with an error. It takes subscriber IDs, not emails, so look people up first; the [sync recipe](recipes.qmd#sync-your-user-table-into-a-list) does that in bulk.

## Single and double opt-in

A single opt-in list accepts a subscription as confirmed the moment it is made. A double opt-in list adds the person as `unconfirmed` and emails them a confirmation link; they receive campaigns only after clicking it.

When your own app has already collected consent (a checkbox on your signup form, say) you can skip the email by passing `pre_confirm=True` to `create_subscriber()`, and `update_subscriber()` always confirms the memberships it sets. When you want Listmonk to run the confirmation flow, leave `pre_confirm` off.

If you run your own confirmation page and want to confirm a double opt-in from code, use [`confirm_optin()`](../reference/confirm_optin.qmd) with the subscriber's and the list's UUIDs:

```python
sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('jane@example.com')
newsletter = listmonk.list_by_id(7)
confirmed = listmonk.confirm_optin(sub.uuid, newsletter.uuid)  # True or False
```

This submits Listmonk's public opt-in form rather than calling a JSON endpoint, so it reports failure as `False` instead of raising. Only call it when the person has genuinely opted in.

## Choosing a list to segment on

Lists are the right tool when membership is a decision someone made or a stage they are in: subscribed to the newsletter, enrolled in a course, invited to the beta. For slicing by a property of the person (city, plan, signup date) you do not need a list at all; store the property in `attribs` and filter with `subscribers(query_text=...)`, as shown in [Subscribers](subscribers.qmd#finding-many). Campaigns can target a list, and Listmonk's own UI can save a query as a segment, so both approaches end up usable from the campaign side.


### Transactional email

Campaigns go to lists. Transactional email goes to one person, right now, because something just happened: a password reset, a receipt, an invitation, a "your export is ready". You write a `tx` template in Listmonk once, then send it from code with the data that fills in the blanks.

## Sending one

```python
ok = listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    'jane@example.com',
    template_id=3,
    template_data={'full_name': 'Jane Doe', 'reset_code': 'abc123'},
    content_type='html',
)
```

[`send_transactional_email()`](../reference/send_transactional_email.qmd) needs a recipient and a template ID. The template must be a `tx` template, not a campaign template; Listmonk keeps the two kinds apart and the ID of a campaign template will not work here. `template_data` is any JSON-serialisable dict. `content_type` is `html`, `markdown`, or `plain` and defaults to `markdown`. `from_email` is optional and falls back to the sender configured on the server.

The return value is `True` when Listmonk accepted the message. Delivery after that point (SMTP errors, bounces) shows up in the Logs section of the Listmonk admin rather than coming back to you.

## Where the data goes

Listmonk renders templates with Go's template engine, not Jinja. Inside a `tx` template your `template_data` is reachable as `.Tx.Data`, and the recipient's record as `.Subscriber`:

```html
<p>Hi {{ .Subscriber.FirstName }},</p>
<p>Your reset code is <strong>{{ .Tx.Data.reset_code }}</strong>.</p>
```

A `tx` template can carry its own subject line, set when you create it; see [Templates](templates.qmd#campaign-templates-and-transactional-templates).

## Plain-text twin, attachments, headers

```python
from pathlib import Path

ok = listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    'jane@example.com',
    template_id=4,
    template_data={'order_id': 1772},
    content_type='html',
    altbody='Your order 1772 has shipped.',
    attachments=[Path('/invoices/1772.pdf')],
    email_headers=[{'X-Priority': '1'}],
)
```

`altbody` is the plain-text alternative for mail clients that prefer text. `attachments` is a list of `Path` objects; the files are read and sent inline as a multipart request, and a path that does not exist raises `ListmonkFileNotFoundError` before anything is sent. Custom `email_headers` are a list of single-entry dicts, one header each, not one dict with many keys.

## People who are not subscribers

By default Listmonk will only send a transactional email to an address that already exists as a subscriber. That is fine for someone who signed up, but your app also emails people who have not: the colleague Jane just invited, the guest who bought one thing, the person who requested a password reset before finishing registration. The `subscriber_mode` argument handles this.

```python
# 'external': no lookup at all. Any address works.
listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    'guest@example.com', template_id=3,
    subscriber_mode='external',
    template_data={'name': 'Sam', 'reset_url': 'https://app.example.com/reset/abc'},
)

# 'fallback': look the subscriber up, but still send if they are not found.
listmonk.send_transactional_email('maybe@example.com', template_id=3, subscriber_mode='fallback')
```

The catch with both modes: only `{{ .Subscriber.Email }}` is populated in the template, because there may be no subscriber record to read from. Anything else the template needs, including the person's name, has to travel in `template_data` and be read as `{{ .Tx.Data.<key> }}`. Templates meant for external sends should be written that way from the start.

Leave `subscriber_mode` out and the field is omitted from the request entirely, so the server keeps its default behaviour. That also means the call works against older Listmonk versions that predate the option.

## Several recipients in one call

Pass a list of addresses instead of a single string:

```python
listmonk.send_transactional_email(
    ['one@example.com', 'two@example.com'],
    template_id=3,
    subscriber_mode='external',
)
```

A single string is sent as Listmonk's `subscriber_email` field and a list as `subscriber_emails`. The server rejects a request that carries both, which is why the client takes one argument that accepts either: the invalid combination cannot be expressed. Blank addresses in the list are dropped, and a list with nothing left raises `ValueError` before any request is made.

## Choosing between transactional and campaign

Reach for transactional email when the trigger is an event in your app and the audience is one person, or a short list of specific people. Reach for a [campaign](campaigns.qmd) when the audience is a list and the content is the same for everyone. Transactional messages do not appear in campaign statistics and are not subject to a campaign's lifecycle; they are sent as soon as Listmonk accepts them.


### Campaigns

A campaign is one message aimed at one or more lists: the newsletter, the launch announcement, the "we changed our pricing" email. Unlike a transactional send it has a life cycle, and the most important thing to know is that creating a campaign does not send it. Sending is a separate, deliberate step, with a test send in between so you can read the result in your own inbox first.

## The life cycle

A campaign is born a `draft`. From there it can become `scheduled` (it will start itself at `send_at`) or `running` (it is sending now). A running campaign can be `paused` and resumed, or `cancelled` for good. When every message has gone out it is `finished`. Those six values are the [`CampaignStatuses`](../reference/models.CampaignStatuses.qmd) enum, and Listmonk only permits certain moves between them: draft to scheduled or running, scheduled back to draft, running to paused or cancelled, paused to running. Ask for anything else and the server answers 400.

## Creating one

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

campaign = listmonk.create_campaign(
    name='June newsletter',
    subject='What shipped in June',
    list_ids={1, 2},
    content_type='markdown',
    body='# Big news\n\nHello there!',
    alt_body='Big news. Hello there!',
    tags=['newsletter'],
    send_at=datetime.now() + timedelta(hours=1),   # optional: schedule it
)
print(campaign.id, campaign.status)  # 42 draft
```

[`create_campaign()`](../reference/create_campaign.qmd) requires a name and a subject; everything else has a default. `list_ids` defaults to `{1}`, Listmonk's default list, so set it. `content_type` is `richtext`, `html`, `markdown`, or `plain`. `template_id` left as `None` means the server's default campaign template. `from_email` falls back to the instance setting and is sent exactly as you write it, so `Newsletter <news@example.com>` keeps its display name. Custom `headers` are a list of single-entry dicts.

`send_at` takes a `datetime`; a naive one is treated as local time when it is serialised. Note that setting `send_at` does not by itself schedule the campaign. It is still a draft until you move it to `scheduled` (see below), at which point Listmonk starts it at that time.

## Attachments

Attaching a file to a campaign is a two-step dance: upload it to Listmonk's media library, then reference its ID.

```python
from pathlib import Path

media = listmonk.upload_media(Path('/reports/june-chart.png'))
# or from bytes: listmonk.upload_media(png_bytes, filename='june-chart.png')

campaign = listmonk.create_campaign('June', 'Our June numbers', media_ids=[media.id])
```

[`upload_media()`](../reference/upload_media.qmd) returns a [`Media`](../reference/models.Media.qmd) model whose `id` goes into `media_ids`. A default Listmonk install only accepts image extensions in the media library; widen Settings, Media, Upload extensions on the server for PDFs and the like. The client does not wrap the endpoints for listing or deleting media, so clean up through the admin UI.

## Changing a draft

```python
campaign = listmonk.campaign_by_id(42)
campaign.subject = 'What shipped in June (and one thing that did not)'
campaign.lists = [1, 2, 5]
campaign = listmonk.update_campaign(campaign)
```

[`update_campaign()`](../reference/update_campaign.qmd) sends the whole campaign back and returns the server's fresh copy. Three things to know:

- Attachments are replaced as a set on every update. With `media_ids` left as `None` the client re-sends the campaign's current attachments so nothing is lost; `media_ids=[]` clears them; a new list swaps them.
- A `send_at` that is already in the past is dropped (sent as `null`) so a stale schedule does not fail the update, and Listmonk then moves a `scheduled` campaign back to `draft`.
- It cannot change the status. Listmonk ignores `status` on this endpoint; use the status calls below.

## Preview

```python
html = listmonk.campaign_preview_by_id(42).preview
```

[`campaign_preview_by_id()`](../reference/campaign_preview_by_id.qmd) returns the campaign rendered through its template as an HTML string, the same thing the admin's preview pane shows. Handy for a last look, or for dropping into a test that checks the merge fields came out right.

## Test before you send

```python
listmonk.test_campaign(42, ['you@example.com', 'editor@example.com'])  # True
```

[`test_campaign()`](../reference/test_campaign.qmd) sends the campaign to the addresses you name and leaves the campaign untouched: still a draft, statistics unchanged. The test copy carries the subject, body, alternate body, custom headers, template, and From address as saved on the server, so what you read is what the list will get.

Every test address must already exist as a subscriber. Listmonk does not create them, and when none of the addresses are known it rejects the request with HTTP 400 ("No known subscribers to test."), which the client raises as `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. Keep yourself on a private "staff" list and this is never a problem.

## Send, pause, cancel

```python
from listmonk.models import CampaignStatuses

listmonk.start_campaign(42)     # draft -> running
listmonk.pause_campaign(42)     # running -> paused
listmonk.start_campaign(42)     # paused -> running again
listmonk.cancel_campaign(42)    # stop for good

listmonk.set_campaign_status(42, CampaignStatuses.scheduled)  # draft -> scheduled, fires at send_at
```

[`start_campaign()`](../reference/start_campaign.qmd), [`pause_campaign()`](../reference/pause_campaign.qmd), and [`cancel_campaign()`](../reference/cancel_campaign.qmd) are thin wrappers over [`set_campaign_status()`](../reference/set_campaign_status.qmd), which talks to Listmonk's dedicated status endpoint. Reach for `set_campaign_status()` directly for the other members of the enum, and always pass the enum rather than a bare string: an unrecognised status reaches Postgres and comes back as an opaque HTTP 500. All four return the updated [`Campaign`](../reference/models.Campaign.qmd), or `None` if no campaign has that ID, and raise `httpx2.HTTPStatusError` for a transition the server refuses.

## Reading progress

The [`Campaign`](../reference/models.Campaign.qmd) model carries `status`, `to_send`, `sent`, `views`, `clicks`, and `started_at`, so a dashboard can poll [`campaign_by_id()`](../reference/campaign_by_id.qmd) while a send runs. [`campaigns()`](../reference/campaigns.qmd) returns every campaign on the instance in one request. Deeper analytics (opens over time, link-level clicks) are not wrapped by this client; use the admin or the Listmonk API directly for those.

## Deleting

```python
listmonk.delete_campaign(42)  # True, or False if there was no such campaign
```

[`delete_campaign()`](../reference/delete_campaign.qmd) looks the campaign up first and returns `False` without issuing a delete when it does not exist.


### Templates

A template is the frame around every message: the header, the footer, the logo, the colours, the unsubscribe link. Campaigns are rendered inside a campaign template, transactional emails inside a `tx` template. You usually design them in Listmonk's editor, but creating and maintaining them from code is useful when you deploy the same look to several instances or keep your templates in version control.

## The one rule

Every template body must contain the placeholder `{{ template "content" . }}` exactly where the message goes. Listmonk renders the campaign body or the transactional message into that spot. [`create_template()`](../reference/create_template.qmd) checks for it and raises `ValueError` before sending anything if it is missing.

```python
body = '''
<html><body>
  <header><img src="https://example.com/logo.png" alt="Example"></header>
  {{ template "content" . }}
  <footer><a href="{{ UnsubscribeURL }}">Unsubscribe</a></footer>
</body></html>
'''
tmpl = listmonk.create_template(name='Brand frame', body=body, type='campaign')
```

Templates use Go's template syntax, so it is `{{ .Subscriber.FirstName }}` and `{{ template "content" . }}`, not Jinja's `{% %}` blocks. The [Listmonk templating docs](https://listmonk.app/docs/templating/) list the functions and fields available.

## Campaign templates and transactional templates

Pass `type='campaign'` or `type='tx'`. A campaign template wraps the campaign body. A `tx` template wraps a transactional message and can carry its own subject line:

```python
reset = listmonk.create_template(
    name='Password reset',
    subject='Your reset code',
    body='<p>Hi {{ .Subscriber.FirstName }}, your code is {{ .Tx.Data.reset_code }}. {{ template "content" . }}</p>',
    type='tx',
)
```

The `tx` template's ID is what you pass to [`send_transactional_email()`](../reference/send_transactional_email.qmd); a campaign template's ID is what you pass to [`create_campaign()`](../reference/create_campaign.qmd). They are not interchangeable.

## Reading and previewing

```python
for tmpl in listmonk.templates():
    print(tmpl.id, tmpl.type, tmpl.name, tmpl.is_default)

tmpl = listmonk.template_by_id(3)          # Template or None
html = listmonk.template_preview_by_id(3).preview
```

[`templates()`](../reference/templates.qmd) returns both kinds in one request. [`template_preview_by_id()`](../reference/template_preview_by_id.qmd) renders the template with lorem-ipsum sample content so you can check the frame without sending anything.

## Updating

```python
tmpl = listmonk.template_by_id(3)
tmpl.body = tmpl.body.replace('2025', '2026')
tmpl = listmonk.update_template(tmpl)
```

[`update_template()`](../reference/update_template.qmd) sends the name, subject, body, and type and returns the re-fetched template. It does not change the default flag; that is a separate call. Note that the placeholder check runs on create only, so keep `{{ template "content" . }}` in the body when you edit it, or the server will reject the update.

## The default template

```python
listmonk.set_default_template(3)   # True, or False if there is no template 3
```

[`set_default_template()`](../reference/set_default_template.qmd) marks a template as the default for its type. A campaign created with `template_id=None` renders with the default campaign template, so this is how you change the look of every campaign that does not pick one explicitly.

## Deleting

```python
listmonk.delete_template(3)  # True, or False if it did not exist
```

Listmonk refuses to delete the default template for a type, which comes back as an `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`; make another template the default first.


### Recipes

Short, copy-ready versions of the jobs most apps need. Each assumes [`set_url_base()`](../reference/set_url_base.qmd) and [`login()`](../reference/login.qmd) already ran at startup, and each links to the guide page that explains the pieces.

## Handle a signup form

Someone ticks "send me the newsletter" on your signup form. They might already be a subscriber (they bought something last year), might be blocklisted (they unsubscribed and came back), or might be new. One function covers all three.

```python
import listmonk
from listmonk.models import SubscriberStatuses

NEWSLETTER = 7


def subscribe_to_newsletter(email: str, name: str, source: str) -> None:
    sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)

    if sub is None:
        listmonk.create_subscriber(email, name, list_ids={NEWSLETTER}, pre_confirm=True,
                                   attribs={'signup_source': source})
        return

    sub.attribs['signup_source'] = source
    # They asked again, so re-enable them even if they had unsubscribed before.
    listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, add_to_lists={NEWSLETTER}, status=SubscriberStatuses.enabled)
```

`pre_confirm=True` because your form collected consent; drop it to let Listmonk run double opt-in instead. The explicit `status=` matters: without it `update_subscriber()` keeps whatever status the person has, which is the right default everywhere except here. See [Subscribers](subscribers.qmd) and [Lists and segmentation](lists.qmd#single-and-double-opt-in).

## Handle an unsubscribe link

Your app has its own unsubscribe page. Decide whether the click means "take me off this one list" or "never email me again"; they are different calls.

```python
def unsubscribe(email: str, list_id: int | None = None) -> bool:
    sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)
    if sub is None:
        return False

    if list_id is not None:
        listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, remove_from_lists={list_id})   # just this list
    else:
        listmonk.block_subscriber(sub)                                  # everything, for good
    return True
```

`block_subscriber()` keeps the record with a `blocklisted` status, so a later import or sync cannot accidentally resurrect them. Use `delete_subscriber()` only for a genuine "forget me" request. See [Pausing, unsubscribing, and deleting](subscribers.qmd#pausing-unsubscribing-and-deleting).

## Send a receipt with a PDF

Receipts go to whoever paid, subscriber or not, so use external mode and carry everything the template needs in `template_data`.

```python
from pathlib import Path

RECEIPT_TEMPLATE = 4  # a 'tx' template


def send_receipt(email: str, order_id: int, total: str, pdf_path: Path) -> bool:
    return listmonk.send_transactional_email(
        email,
        RECEIPT_TEMPLATE,
        subscriber_mode='external',
        template_data={'order_id': order_id, 'total': total},
        attachments=[pdf_path],
        content_type='html',
        altbody=f'Thanks for order {order_id}. Your receipt is attached.',
    )
```

In external mode only `{{ .Subscriber.Email }}` is available, so the template reads the order number as `{{ .Tx.Data.order_id }}`. See [Transactional email](transactional-email.qmd#people-who-are-not-subscribers).

## Send a password reset

Same idea, minus the attachment. Use `fallback` if most of your users are subscribers and you still want their name available when they are:

```python
RESET_TEMPLATE = 3


def send_password_reset(email: str, reset_url: str) -> bool:
    return listmonk.send_transactional_email(
        email,
        RESET_TEMPLATE,
        subscriber_mode='fallback',
        template_data={'reset_url': reset_url},
        content_type='html',
    )
```

Remember that in `fallback` mode the subscriber fields other than the email are empty when the lookup fails, so write the template to work with `{{ .Tx.Data.reset_url }}` and a generic greeting.

## Sync your user table into a list

A nightly job that makes sure every active customer is on the "customers" list, creating anyone Listmonk has not seen yet.

```python
CUSTOMERS = 9


def sync_customers(users: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> None:
    """users is a list of (email, name) pairs from your own database."""
    ids: list[int] = []
    for email, name in users:
        sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)
        if sub is None:
            sub = listmonk.create_subscriber(email, name, pre_confirm=True)
        ids.append(sub.id)

    for start in range(0, len(ids), 500):
        listmonk.add_subscribers_to_lists(ids[start:start + 500], [CUSTOMERS])
```

`add_subscribers_to_lists()` takes IDs, de-duplicates them, and returns `False` rather than raising on an error, so check it if you need to. People already on the list are simply left there. This loop makes one lookup per user; for a very large table, pull everyone with `subscribers()` once and build a dict by email instead. See [Lists and segmentation](lists.qmd#membership).

## Send a newsletter from code

Create, attach, test, then start. Keep yourself on a private staff list so the test send always has a known subscriber to go to.

```python
from pathlib import Path

NEWSLETTER = 7
STAFF = ['you@example.com']


def send_newsletter(subject: str, markdown_body: str, chart: Path) -> int:
    media = listmonk.upload_media(chart)
    campaign = listmonk.create_campaign(
        name=subject, subject=subject, list_ids={NEWSLETTER},
        content_type='markdown', body=markdown_body, media_ids=[media.id],
    )
    listmonk.test_campaign(campaign.id, STAFF)
    input(f'Test sent to {STAFF}. Press Enter to send campaign {campaign.id} to the list...')
    listmonk.start_campaign(campaign.id)
    return campaign.id
```

Swap the `input()` for whatever approval step fits your workflow. To schedule instead of sending now, pass `send_at=` to `create_campaign()` and move the campaign to `CampaignStatuses.scheduled` with `set_campaign_status()`. See [Campaigns](campaigns.qmd).

## Add a health check to your app

```python
import httpx2


def listmonk_ok() -> bool:
    return listmonk.is_healthy(timeout_config=httpx2.Timeout(timeout=3))
```

`is_healthy()` never raises; it returns `False` for an unreachable server, a rejected credential, or a client that was never configured, so it is safe to call from a readiness probe. The short timeout keeps the probe fast when the mail server is down. See [Errors and troubleshooting](error-handling.qmd#timeouts).



## Under the hood

### Testing your integration

Your app's tests should not send real email, and they should not need a Listmonk server running on the CI machine. The library makes that easy because of how it is built: every request goes through the module-level `httpx2.get`, `httpx2.post`, `httpx2.put`, and `httpx2.delete` functions. Patch those four and the whole client talks to whatever you put behind them.

This is exactly how the library's own suite works. The pattern below is a trimmed version of its `tests/conftest.py`.

## A fake server in forty lines

```python
import functools
from typing import Any
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

import httpx2
import pytest

from listmonk import impl


class FakeListmonk:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.routes: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, Any]] = {}
        self.requests: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    def respond(self, method: str, path: str, *, json: Any = None, status_code: int = 200) -> None:
        self.routes[(method.upper(), path)] = (status_code, json)

    def handle(self, method: str, url: str, **kwargs: Any) -> httpx2.Response:
        path = urlsplit(url).path
        self.requests.append({'method': method, 'path': path, 'url': url, **kwargs})
        status_code, body = self.routes[(method, path)]
        request = httpx2.Request(method, url)
        return httpx2.Response(status_code, request=request, json=body)


@pytest.fixture
def fake_listmonk(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> FakeListmonk:
    server = FakeListmonk()
    for verb in ('get', 'post', 'put', 'delete'):
        monkeypatch.setattr(httpx2, verb, functools.partial(server.handle, verb.upper()))
    # Skip the login round trip: put the client straight into the logged-in state.
    monkeypatch.setattr(impl, 'url_base', 'https://listmonk.test')
    monkeypatch.setattr(impl, 'username', 'api')
    monkeypatch.setattr(impl, 'password', 'token')
    monkeypatch.setattr(impl, 'has_logged_in', True)
    return server
```

Returning real `httpx2.Response` objects matters. The client calls `raise_for_status()` and `.json()` on them, so a status code of 4xx in `respond()` produces a genuine `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`, and your error-handling code is exercised for real.

## Using it

```python
def test_signup_creates_a_new_subscriber(fake_listmonk):
    # Lookup finds nobody, then the create succeeds.
    fake_listmonk.respond('GET', '/api/subscribers', json={'data': {'results': [], 'total': 0}})
    fake_listmonk.respond('POST', '/api/subscribers', json={'data': {
        'id': 7, 'email': 'jane@example.com', 'name': 'Jane', 'status': 'enabled',
        'created_at': '2026-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z', 'lists': [], 'attribs': {},
    }})

    subscribe_to_newsletter('jane@example.com', 'Jane', source='test')

    post = next(r for r in fake_listmonk.requests if r['method'] == 'POST')
    assert post['json']['email'] == 'jane@example.com'
    assert post['json']['lists'] == [7]
```

Assert on the recorded request when the interesting part is what your code asked Listmonk to do, and on the return value when the interesting part is how your code reacted. Both are available.

## Shapes the fake has to produce

The client expects Listmonk's real response envelopes, so the fake has to speak them:

- Collection endpoints (`/api/subscribers`, `/api/lists`, `/api/campaigns`) wrap results as `{'data': {'results': [...], 'total': N}}`. `subscribers()` pages until `total` is reached, so set `total` to the number of results you return unless you are testing pagination.
- `/api/templates` is the exception and returns a flat list: `{'data': [...]}`.
- Single-item endpoints return `{'data': {...}}`. Deletes and status endpoints return `{'data': true}`.
- Campaign and template previews return raw HTML, not JSON. `httpx2.Response(200, request=request, text='<h1>Hi</h1>')` does it.
- The direct subscriber endpoint `/api/subscribers/{id}` answers an unknown ID with status 400; the client turns that into `None`.
- Timestamps are ISO strings such as `'2026-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z'`; the models parse them into `datetime` objects.

## What the library's own tests check

If you want to see the full version, the repository's [tests](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/listmonk/tree/main/tests) run every public function against an in-memory fake with canned payloads shaped like real Listmonk responses. They are a good source of realistic JSON when you need a `Campaign` or `Subscriber` body for your own fixtures.

## Integration tests against a real instance

For an occasional end-to-end check, the repository's `example_client/client.py` exercises every major operation against a live Listmonk, reading its settings from a local JSON file. Run it against a staging instance with a throwaway list rather than production; it creates and deletes subscribers, lists, campaigns, and templates as it goes.


### How it works

Knowing what the client does on your behalf explains most of its behaviour, including the parts that look surprising at first.

## One module, one instance

`listmonk` keeps its configuration in four module-level variables: the base URL, the username, the password, and a logged-in flag. [`set_url_base()`](../reference/set_url_base.qmd) sets the first, [`login()`](../reference/login.qmd) sets the rest after validating the credentials against the health endpoint, and every other function checks the flag before doing anything and raises `OperationNotAllowedError` if it is not set.

Two consequences follow. A process talks to one Listmonk instance at a time; to switch, call `set_url_base()` and `login()` again, and the new credentials are re-validated rather than trusted. And changing credentials is not thread-safe: do the configuration once at startup, before worker threads start, and leave it alone. Reads from worker threads are fine, since the variables never change after that.

## Every call is a fresh request

The client uses httpx2's module-level functions (`httpx2.get()`, `httpx2.post()`, and so on) rather than a long-lived `Client`. Each call opens its own connection, sends HTTP Basic auth built from the stored credentials, follows redirects, identifies itself with a `User-Agent` of the form `Listmonk-Client v0.7.33 / Python 3.14.0 / Darwin`, and times out after 10 seconds unless you pass `timeout_config`. There is no connection pooling and no session state, which is why a fake server for tests only needs to patch those four functions.

The trade-off is a little more latency per call. For a handful of calls per request in a web app it is unnoticeable; for a loop over tens of thousands of subscribers, batch where the API allows it (`add_subscribers_to_lists()` takes many IDs at once) and pull data in bulk with `subscribers()` rather than one lookup at a time.

## Pagination

[`subscribers()`](../reference/subscribers.qmd) asks for 500 records per page and keeps going until the server's `total` is reached, so one call can be several requests. [`lists()`](../reference/lists.qmd), [`campaigns()`](../reference/campaigns.qmd), and [`templates()`](../reference/templates.qmd) ask for one very large page and make a single request.

## Lookups by email and UUID are SQL filters

Listmonk has a direct endpoint for fetching a subscriber by ID, and [`subscriber_by_id()`](../reference/subscriber_by_id.qmd) uses it. It has no direct endpoint for email or UUID, so [`subscriber_by_email()`](../reference/subscriber_by_email.qmd) and [`subscriber_by_uuid()`](../reference/subscriber_by_uuid.qmd) send a `query` parameter that Listmonk runs as a SQL expression inside a read-only transaction. That is why those two need the `subscribers:sql_query` permission, and why the client quotes the value as a SQL literal with embedded quotes escaped before sending it.

## Models

Responses are parsed into Pydantic models in `listmonk.models`: [`Subscriber`](../reference/models.Subscriber.qmd), [`MailingList`](../reference/models.MailingList.qmd), [`Campaign`](../reference/models.Campaign.qmd), [`Template`](../reference/models.Template.qmd), and [`Media`](../reference/models.Media.qmd), plus the enums [`SubscriberStatuses`](../reference/models.SubscriberStatuses.qmd) and [`CampaignStatuses`](../reference/models.CampaignStatuses.qmd). Fields the server may omit are `Optional`. Timestamps are `datetime` objects.

The update functions do not send those response models back as-is. `update_subscriber()` builds a `CreateSubscriberModel` from the fields Listmonk's PUT accepts, `update_campaign()` builds an `UpdateCampaignModel` (which is where a past `send_at` gets dropped), and `update_template()` builds a `CreateTemplateModel`. Those request models are public too, in case you want to see exactly what goes over the wire.

## Response validation

Every JSON call runs the response through one helper: raise `httpx2.HTTPStatusError` for a 4xx or 5xx, raise `ValidationError` for an empty body or a body that is not JSON, otherwise hand back the parsed dict. Previews are the exception, since Listmonk returns them as raw HTML.

## What the client does not cover

Listmonk's API is larger than this client. Not wrapped, as of this version: campaign analytics, campaign archives, bounces, bulk subscriber deletion and blocklisting by query, listing and deleting media, importing subscribers from files, settings, and user management. Transactional sends by subscriber ID (rather than email) are also not exposed. For any of those, call the [Listmonk API](https://listmonk.app/docs/apis/apis/) directly with httpx2 and the same Basic auth; the base URL and credentials you gave the client are available as `listmonk.get_base_url()` and the `username` and `password` attributes of `listmonk.impl`.

An async variant is planned but not yet implemented. With httpx2 underneath, the shape of it is clear; it is a matter of doing the work.

## Version and user agent

`listmonk.__version__` reports the installed package version, read from the package metadata, and `listmonk.user_agent` is the string sent with every request.
